141.title: Ask what's needed
141.hook: good service asks first instead of assuming
141.howItsDone: Many relief organizations ask communities what they need, or give cash so people can choose, and volunteer programs often train helpers to ask before acting.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the helper's high, and the honest link between helping and feeling better. Your line was it comes back. Did it? Day one hundred forty-one.

After big disasters, something strange often happens. People everywhere want to help, so they pack boxes: old coats, canned food, stuffed animals, and ship them off. And the boxes pile up. Relief workers have to sort them, store them, sometimes throw them away, while what the place actually needed was clean water, cash, or a specific medicine. Aid workers have a grim nickname for it: the second disaster. Every one of those boxes was packed with love. And almost none of the packers asked first. Today's practice is ask what's needed.
screen: `BOXES OF OLD COATS.` → `THE SECOND DISASTER.` → `ASK WHAT'S NEEDED.`

segments.voice: There's a small, striking scene in the Gospel of Mark. Jesus is leaving the town of Jericho, and a blind man named Bartimaeus is sitting by the road, shouting for help. The crowd tells him to be quiet. Jesus stops, calls him over, and asks him a question that sounds almost odd: "What wilt thou that I should do unto thee?" The need seems obvious. The man is blind. But Jesus asks anyway, and Bartimaeus answers in his own words: that I might receive my sight. Christians have long noticed that question. Whatever you believe about the story, there's a lesson in the asking. It treats the person as the expert on their own life. It doesn't assume. The same idea runs through modern service, in a very different setting. In the disability rights movement, a slogan spread in the nineteen nineties: nothing about us without us. Don't design for people without asking them. Good aid groups now often give cash, because people usually know better than donors what they need. And it scales all the way down to your kitchen. A friend has a new baby. You could bring lasagna, and that might be lovely. Or you could ask, and learn that what they really want is someone to walk the dog, or hold the baby for an hour so they can shower. Asking takes a little humility. It admits you don't already know. But it turns help from something you give into something you do together.
screen: `WHAT WILT THOU?` · `THE PERSON IS THE EXPERT.` · `NOTHING ABOUT US WITHOUT US.` · `LASAGNA, OR THE DOG?` · then, large: `ASK FIRST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan one question. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone going through something: a new job, an illness, a move, a loss. Notice what you assumed they need. Now set that assumption down. Picture yourself asking, simply: what would actually help right now? Picture waiting for the answer, even if it surprises you. The bell holds the time.
Ask what's needed. Good service asks first, and treats the person as the expert on their own life. Today's word.
Your line: ask first. Today, ask one person what would help, and do that, not what you'd planned. Day one hundred forty-one.

142.title: Small and regular
142.hook: a small weekly act tends to last longer than a rare grand one
142.howItsDone: Many people of every faith and none keep a standing weekly slot for service, like a Tuesday shift at a shelter or a regular visit to a neighbor, so it happens without deciding each time.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the blind man by the road, and the question that came first. Your line was ask first. What did someone tell you they needed? Day one hundred forty-two.

Picture two people. The first, once a year, does something huge: runs a marathon for charity, flies across the world to build a school. Photos, speeches, a glow that lasts a month. The second visits the same elderly neighbor every Tuesday for twenty minutes. No photos. Nobody claps. Ten years later, which one has changed more, in the world and in themselves? This week we planned one act of service, gave without being seen, noticed what helping gives back, and learned to ask first. Today we put it on a rhythm. Today's practice is small and regular.
screen: `THE ONCE-A-YEAR MARATHON.` → `EVERY TUESDAY, TWENTY MINUTES.` → `SMALL AND REGULAR.`

segments.voice: Two old voices say something surprisingly similar here, each from inside its own tradition. In Islam, a well-known hadith, recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, tells that the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, was asked which deeds are most beloved to God. His answer: the ones done most regularly, even if they are small. And Maimonides, whose ladder of giving we climbed earlier this week, makes a related point in his commentary on a teaching in the Mishnah. Giving a thousand coins to one person in one go, he says, doesn't shape your character the way giving one coin a thousand times does. The repetition is what trains the heart. Each tradition has its own reasons, rooted in its own faith, and they aren't saying the same thing in the same way. But they meet on a very practical point. The grand gesture happens to you once. The small, regular act happens a hundred times, and slowly it changes who you are. It's also just more likely to last. A huge commitment is easy to start and hard to keep; when life gets busy, it's the first thing to go. A small one fits into a real week. That's why this week's practice was never one heroic day. It was one act a week. And the simplest trick for keeping it is almost boring: give it a slot. Same day, same time. Put it in the calendar the way you would a dentist appointment. Then, when the day comes, you don't have to decide. You just go.
screen: `SMALL, IF DONE REGULARLY.` · `ONE COIN A THOUSAND TIMES.` · `SMALL ACTS LAST LONGER.` · `GIVE IT A SLOT.` · then, large: `SAME TIME NEXT WEEK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find next week's slot. Settle, and breathe. Look back at this week: the act you planned, the anonymous gift, the question you asked. Which one could repeat? Now picture next week's calendar. Pick a day and an hour that's usually free. See yourself there, doing the same small thing again. Let it feel ordinary, like brushing your teeth. That's the goal. The bell holds the time.
Small and regular. A small weekly act, given a fixed slot, tends to last longer than a rare grand one. Today's word.
Your line: same time next week. Today, put next week's act in your calendar, with a day and an hour. And tomorrow, a week of rest begins. Day one hundred forty-two.

143.title: The sabbath idea
143.hook: Judaism's weekly day of rest, rooted in creation and the commandments (Genesis 2:2–3; Exodus 20:8–11)
143.howItsDone: Many Jews keep Shabbat from Friday sunset to Saturday nightfall, lighting candles, sharing meals and prayer, and refraining from the kinds of work Jewish law describes; practice varies across Orthodox, Conservative, Reform and secular Jews.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the small act on a regular slot. Your line was same time next week. Is it in the calendar? Day one hundred forty-three.

It's Friday, just before sunset, in a Jewish home. The cooking is done. The table is set. Someone lights two candles. Phones, for many families, go off and stay off. For the next twenty-five hours or so, until three stars appear on Saturday night, there will be no shopping, no work emails, no building anything. Just meals, prayer, walks, naps, conversation. For thousands of years, Jews have stopped the world like this, every single week. A new week of our path starts here, with rest, and it starts with the original. Today's word is Shabbat.

Shabbat comes from a Hebrew root that means to stop, to cease. It's rooted in the very first pages of the Torah. In Genesis, after six days of creation, God finishes the work, rests on the seventh day, and blesses it and makes it holy. Later, in the Ten Commandments, the command comes plainly: "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy." And it isn't only for the family. The text includes servants, animals and the stranger in town: everyone gets the day. Interestingly, the Torah gives two reasons in two places. In Exodus, the reason is creation: God rested, so you rest. In Deuteronomy, the reason is freedom: remember you were slaves in Egypt, and slaves never get a day off. What counts as work? The rabbis of the Mishnah listed thirty-nine kinds, drawn from the tasks of building the sanctuary in the wilderness: sowing, baking, sewing, writing, building, kindling a fire. Notice what they share. They're all kinds of making. Shabbat is a day off from making: from changing the world, and simply living in it. The twentieth-century rabbi Abraham Joshua Heschel described it as a palace built in time rather than in space. The Jewish Sabbath has its own laws, its own prayers and its own meaning, and it belongs to the Jewish people. This week, the path only borrows the idea underneath it, with respect: that a person needs a regular stretch where nothing has to be produced.
screen: `SHABBAT: TO STOP.` · `REMEMBER THE SABBATH DAY.` · `CREATION, AND FREEDOM.` · `THIRTY-NINE KINDS OF MAKING.` · then, large: `A DAY OFF FROM MAKING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pick one rest window this week. Settle, and breathe. Look at the week ahead. Find a stretch, an evening, a morning, a few hours, where you could stop making things: no work, no errands, no fixing, no producing. Picture when it begins, maybe with a small sign, like switching off a lamp or a phone. Picture what you'll do instead: eat, walk, talk, nap. The bell holds the time.
Shabbat. Judaism's weekly day of rest, from a Hebrew root for stopping, kept from Friday sunset to Saturday night. Today's word.
Your line: a day off from making. Today, choose your rest window for this week, and tell one person when it is. Day one hundred forty-three.

144.title: An hour without the phone
144.howItsDone: People who keep a tech sabbath often start with one screen-free hour, putting the phone in a drawer or another room, and lengthen it over weeks toward an evening or a full day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shabbat, from a Hebrew root for stopping. Your line was a day off from making. When is your rest window this week? Day one hundred forty-four.

Quick test. Where's your phone right now? If you're listening to this, probably in your hand. Fair enough. But think about the rest of the day. On the table at dinner. On the pillow at night. In your pocket on a walk, buzzing against your leg, or not buzzing, and you check anyway. A whole day off, like the Sabbath we met yesterday, can sound impossible from here. So we're not starting with a day. We're starting with sixty minutes, and a piece of furniture. Today's practice is an hour without the phone.
screen: `WHERE'S YOUR PHONE?` → `NOT A DAY. AN HOUR.` → `AN HOUR WITHOUT THE PHONE.`

segments.voice: Here's a surprising finding. In a 2017 study at the University of Texas, people did tests of attention and memory with their phone in one of three places: on the desk, face down; in a pocket or bag; or in another room. Phones were silent the whole time. The people whose phones were in another room did best. The researchers called the effect brain drain: part of your mind stays busy not checking the phone. Later studies have found smaller or mixed effects, so hold it loosely. But the lesson most people recognize from their own lives is simple. Face down isn't away. Silent isn't away. Away is away. That's why the practice has a drawer in it. Out of sight works better than willpower, because you're not spending the hour resisting. You've just made it a little harder to reach. There's a modern movement that took this straight from the Sabbath. In 2010, a Jewish nonprofit started a National Day of Unplugging, and writers and families since have kept what some call a tech sabbath: one day a week without screens. That's the destination this week. But nearly everyone who does it says the same thing: start smaller than you think. One hour. Pick one that's easy, like a walk or cooking dinner. Put the phone in a drawer, or another room, and close it. You'll probably reach for your pocket a few times. That's the habit showing itself. Let the hand come back empty.
screen: `THREE PLACES FOR THE PHONE.` · `FACE DOWN ISN'T AWAY.` · `A TECH SABBATH.` · `START WITH ONE HOUR.` · then, large: `THE DRAWER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rehearse your hour. When this session ends, notice where your phone will go. For now, settle, and breathe. Picture the drawer, or the other room. Picture sliding the phone in and closing it. Notice what your body does: a small tightening, maybe, or relief. Now picture the hour itself, the room quiet, your hands free. Choose which hour today it will be. The bell holds the time.
An hour without the phone. Not face down, not silent: out of sight, for sixty minutes, the first step toward a weekly rest. Today's word.
screen: `AN HOUR WITHOUT THE PHONE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the drawer. Today, put your phone in a drawer, or another room, for one hour. When your hand reaches for it, let it come back empty. Day one hundred forty-four.

145.title: What fills the space
145.howItsDone: People who try a screen-free stretch often describe restless boredom at first, followed by more noticing and daydreaming, and many deliberately let themselves be bored instead of reaching for a device.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the phone went away for an hour. Your line was the drawer. How many times did your hand reach for it? Day one hundred forty-five.

If you did the hour, you probably met something. Not peace, at first. Something itchier. Around minute ten, a kind of restless flatness: nothing to do, nothing to look at, the clock suddenly very slow. You may have found yourself reorganizing a shelf, or standing in front of the fridge with no plan. That feeling is boredom, and most of us have arranged our whole lives so we never have to feel it for more than about four seconds. Today we look it in the eye. Today's practice is what fills the space.
screen: `MINUTE TEN.` → `STANDING AT THE FRIDGE.` → `WHAT FILLS THE SPACE.`

segments.voice: In the sixteen hundreds, the French mathematician Blaise Pascal wrote a line that sounds like it was written about phones. He said he'd discovered that all of people's unhappiness comes from one thing, "that they cannot stay quietly in their own chamber." We chase distractions, he said, so we never have to sit alone with ourselves. In 2014, psychologists tested this almost literally. They asked people to sit alone in a plain room for six to fifteen minutes with nothing but their thoughts. Many found it unpleasant. In one version, people could press a button to give themselves a mild electric shock, and a surprising number did, rather than just sit there: about two in three men, and one in four women. Boredom is uncomfortable. That's real. But here's the other side. In a different study, people who first did something dull, copying numbers out of a phone book, then came up with more creative ideas than people who hadn't. Boredom seems to push the mind to go looking. And that's the whole practice this week. Boredom is not the end of the story. It's the hallway. If you don't grab the phone, the restlessness peaks, and then, slowly, the mind starts to notice things. The sound of the fridge. The light on the wall. A thought you haven't had time for in months. What fills the space isn't nothing. It's usually you. Bored is the door. Most people just never wait long enough to walk through.
screen: `PASCAL: STAY IN YOUR ROOM.` · `THE BUTTON IN THE EMPTY ROOM.` · `BORED, THEN MORE CREATIVE.` · `THE RESTLESSNESS PEAKS, THEN FADES.` · then, large: `BORED IS THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a small rehearsal of boredom. For this sit, don't follow your breath, don't count, don't do anything clever. Just sit, eyes open, and let it be dull. Notice the itch to do something. Let it rise. Don't scratch it. Watch what comes after: a sound, a color, a thought. Just notice what fills the space. The bell holds the time.
What fills the space. When the screen goes away, boredom comes first, and if you wait, noticing comes after. Today's word.
Your line: bored is the door. Today, stay bored for five minutes on purpose: in a line, on a bus, at the kitchen table. Don't fill it. See what comes. Day one hundred forty-five.

146.title: A screen-free meal
146.hook: eat with the people, not the feed
146.howItsDone: Many families keep a no-phones rule at the dinner table, and many religious communities share regular meals, like Shabbat dinner, langar and iftar, where the meal itself is the gathering.

segments.voice: Yesterday, boredom, and what comes after it. Your line was bored is the door. What did you notice once the itch passed? Day one hundred forty-six.

Look around a restaurant sometime. A couple at a table for two, both looking down, faces lit blue. A family of four, each on a separate screen, the food going cold. Maybe you've been one of them; most of us have. Nobody meant to. The phone was just there, face up by the fork, and it buzzed. Now picture the opposite: a table where the only lights are the lamp and people's faces, and the conversation wanders wherever it wants. For most of history, that was just what dinner was. Today's practice is a screen-free meal.
screen: `FACES LIT BLUE.` → `THE PHONE BY THE FORK.` → `A SCREEN-FREE MEAL.`

segments.voice: Start with a word. Companion comes from Latin: com, with, and panis, bread. A companion is literally someone you share bread with. The meal is where we've always made each other into companions. Across traditions, the shared table is sacred ground, each for its own reasons: the Shabbat dinner we met this week, the Sikh langar, the Muslim iftar that breaks the Ramadan fast together, the Christian meal of bread and wine, the Hindu offering of food before it's eaten. Now, the phone. In a 2012 study in England, pairs of strangers talked for ten minutes. For some, a phone sat nearby on the table; for others, a notebook. Nobody touched the phone. But when the phone was there, especially during meaningful conversations, people later felt less close to their partner and trusted them less. Just its presence seemed to put part of the listener somewhere else. In another study, friends eating dinner out with phones on the table enjoyed the meal a little less than friends with phones put away. These are small effects, from a handful of studies. But they match what many of us feel. A phone on the table says, quietly, someone more important might call. Put it away, and the table says something else: right now, you're the ones I'm with. And a screen-free meal isn't only for families. Eating alone counts too. Taste the food. Look out the window. You can be good company for yourself.
screen: `COMPANION: WITH BREAD.` · `THE SHARED TABLE, EVERYWHERE.` · `THE PHONE NOBODY TOUCHED.` · `YOU'RE THE ONES I'M WITH.` · then, large: `EAT WITH THEM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan one meal with no screens. Settle, and breathe. Which meal today or tomorrow could be screen-free? Picture the table, and who's there, or just you. Picture putting the phones in another room, TV off. Picture the first bite, and actually tasting it. Picture one question you might ask someone across the table, or one thing you'd notice alone. The bell holds the time.
A screen-free meal. Phones away, TV off: eating with the people in front of you, not the feed. Today's word.
Your line: eat with them. Today, make one meal screen-free. Phones in another room. If someone asks why, tell them it's an experiment. Day one hundred forty-six.

147.title: Your weekly rest
147.hook: design your digital sabbath: when, how long, what instead
147.howItsDone: People who keep a digital sabbath usually set a regular weekly window, often an evening or a weekend day, put devices away, and plan what they'll do instead, like walks, meals, reading or rest.

segments.voice: Yesterday, companions, bread, and the phone nobody touched. Your line was eat with them. Which meal went screen-free? Day one hundred forty-seven.

Here's the week in one breath. Shabbat, the original weekly rest: a day off from making. Then one hour, phone in a drawer. Then the boredom that comes first, and the noticing after. Then one meal, eaten with the people instead of the feed. Now for the part that turns it from an experiment into a habit. You're going to design your own weekly rest. But first, one thing gets in almost everybody's way, and it's worth naming. It's the voice that says: you haven't done enough to deserve a break yet. Today's practice is your weekly rest.
screen: `SHABBAT, THE DRAWER, BOREDOM, THE MEAL.` → `NOT DONE ENOUGH YET?` → `YOUR WEEKLY REST.`

segments.voice: Notice something about the Sabbath we met at the start of this week. It doesn't wait for you to finish. It arrives at sunset on Friday whether the work is done or not. The medieval commentator Rashi, reading the command to work six days and do all your work, explains it this way: when the Sabbath comes, it should feel as if all your work is done. Not because it is. Because you're allowed to stop anyway. The Gospels have their own saying about it, in a different setting: "The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath." Each tradition keeps rest in its own way and for its own reasons. But both push against the same modern habit: treating rest as a prize for productivity. Rest isn't earned. It's part of the week. So, the design. Three questions. First, when? Pick a regular slot, like Saturday morning, or Sunday after lunch, or every weeknight after eight. Regular matters more than long. Second, how long? Start with what you'll actually keep. Three hours you keep beats a whole day you abandon. You can grow it. Third, and this is the one people forget: what instead? An empty rest fills right back up with scrolling. So choose what goes in the space: a walk, a long meal, a book, a nap, friends, prayer if you pray. Write down all three. A rest with a time, a length and a plan is much harder to skip than a vague good intention.
screen: `IT ARRIVES WHETHER YOU'RE DONE.` · `AS IF ALL YOUR WORK IS DONE.` · `WHEN, AND HOW LONG?` · `WHAT GOES IN INSTEAD?` · then, large: `REST ISN'T EARNED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: design your rest. Settle, and breathe. First, when: let a day and a time appear. Say it inside. Second, how long: pick a length you'd actually keep. Say it. Third, what instead: choose two things that will fill the space. Picture the rest beginning: phone into the drawer, a lamp on, a deep breath. Notice if the voice says you haven't earned it. Let it talk. Rest anyway. The bell holds the time.
Your weekly rest. A regular, screen-free stretch with a time, a length and a plan for what goes in it. Today's word.
Your line: rest isn't earned. Today, write your weekly rest down: when, how long, what instead. Put it somewhere you'll see it. Next week, we watch the sun go down. Day one hundred forty-seven.

fork.setup: it's time for your weekly rest, and your to-do list isn't finished. what does today's teaching say?
options: finish the list first; then you've earned it.
rest anyway, as if the work were done.
skip rest this week and double it next week.
fork.reveal: rest anyway. as Rashi reads it, when the Sabbath comes it should feel as if all your work is done. rest isn't earned.

original.note: Hebrew, menuchah: rest, repose. a word often used for the special rest of the Sabbath.

trapdoor: what you thought: rest is a reward for a productive week.
what it means: rest is part of the week, and it comes whether or not the work is done.
what a scholar hears: Rashi on Exodus 20:9 ('as if all your work were done'), drawing on the Mekhilta; and Mark 2:27.

sources.ref: Rashi on Exodus 20:9 (drawing on the Mekhilta)
